nameStory: The scientific name 'convexum' refers to this tiny spider's distinctly curved or dome-shaped carapace (the hard front section of its body). While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, spider experts sometimes call it the 'domed sheetweb weaver' for its rounded appearance and distinctive web-building style.
description: This is an extremely small spider, barely visible to the naked eye at just 2-3mm long. The domed sheetweb weaver belongs to a family of tiny spiders that create delicate sheet-like webs close to the ground. Its most notable feature is the distinctly curved, dome-shaped front section of its body, which gives it an almost hunchbacked appearance when viewed from the side. Like other sheetweb weavers, it has long, thin legs relative to its tiny body size.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The front section (carapace) is distinctly dome-shaped or convex, creating a small hump that you can see even with a hand lens

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny at 2-3mm - smaller than most ants and barely visible without magnification

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates delicate, flat sheet webs stretched horizontally close to the ground or in low vegetation, feeling gossamer-thin if accidentally touched

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale brownish to yellowish body color that blends easily with dead leaves and soil

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Long, thin legs that appear disproportionately lengthy compared to the tiny body

habitat: Found in leaf litter, low vegetation, and ground cover in forests and woodland edges. Prefers moist, sheltered spots under logs, rocks, or among fallen leaves where its tiny sheet webs can be anchored close to the soil surface. Most likely encountered in deciduous or mixed forests with rich, organic soil layers.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to construct their delicate sheet webs in the leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and spiders are actively hunting small prey like springtails and tiny flies.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced before adults die off with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Eggs overwinter in protected locations, with the next generation emerging the following spring.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region, making any sighting a potentially significant scientific discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tiny sheetweb weavers in the same family, but the distinctly domed carapace sets it apart. Remember: if the spider's 'forehead' looks like a tiny helmet or dome, you might have found this rare species.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England (only one recorded observation) suggests it may be at the edge of its natural range here, or that it's simply so small and secretive that it's been overlooked by most observers.
compareHints: Since this is the only Porrhomma species recorded in New England, compare it with other tiny sheetweb weavers like Erigone species. The key difference is the pronounced dome-shaped carapace - other small linyphiids have flatter, less curved front body sections. Its distinctly convex profile makes it unique among New England's minute spiders.
